children: has secured U.S. regulatory approval for its 737 MAX 10, bringing the planemaker closer to starting deliveries of the largest aircraft in its single-aisle MAX lineup after a prolonged certification process.
The company had originally targeted 2020 for the first deliveries, but technical challenges and increased regulatory scrutiny extended the timeline.

MAX program has faced greater oversight since two fatal crashes involving the 737 MAX 8 in 2018 and 2019 and a January 2024 incident in which a cabin panel detached from an Alaska Airlines 737 MAX 9 during flight. More recently, a navigation software issue added another hurdle to the MAX 10's approval process, although the Federal Aviation Administration determined that the glitch did not pose a safety concern.

said the MAX 10's certification involved more than 2,000 hours of flight testing and 1,000 hours of ground tests, alongside detailed safety reviews and documentation. The aircraft is the first commercial jet to receive certification under the full requirements of the 2020 Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act, which strengthened documentation requirements for safety assessments and human factors evaluations.
The company has received 1,555 orders for the MAX 10 from more than 30 customers, representing over 30% of the MAX family's current order book. Boeing
expects deliveries to begin in the coming months.
The aircraft is expected to support Boeing’s
financial recovery, while delays have helped Airbus’
A321neo gain ground in the large single-aisle market.

The aircraft can seat up to 230 passengers in a maximum-capacity configuration. In a typical two-class layout, it accommodates 185 to 210 passengers and has a range of up to 3,100 nautical miles (5,740 km), according to Boeing
